_README: The fit re-swept on the app's own tune, where the app's ratios are actually
fitted so the top gear really is 0.82 and the axis reads 159. First time
the axis, the fit and the gearbox have all belonged to the same setup.
IT RESOLVES E2, AND IT DOES SO BY MAKING THE QUESTION THE WRONG ONE.
tune: the app's tune, tire pressure still at 50 psi

held.ratiosNote: the APP's ratio set, applied — so SPREAD[7]'s top gear of 0.82 is genuinely on the car for these rows

fitNote: Boston swept to 4.53, 4.52 and 4.51 and did not state which one he judged as just touching the edge. It barely matters — see kIsTheInvariant, where the three differ by 0.44% in k — but the row should say which, so it is left null rather than guessed.
kIsTheInvariant: E2 IS RESOLVED, AND THE ANSWER IS THAT THE QUESTION WAS WRONG. Neither 157
nor 159 was a misreading, and it does not matter which is 'the' axis.
k = axisMax * fit * topRatio
Everything lands between 588.1 and 590.7 — a spread of 0.44% across two
builds, three tunes, two axis readings and two weeks.
THE MECHANISM: WHEN THE AXIS MOVES, THE FIT MOVES TO COMPENSATE. The axis
is the chart's scale; the fit is the final drive at which the top gear
reaches the end of that scale. A longer scale needs a shorter final drive
to reach it, and the product is conserved. So k is the physical constant —
speed at redline per unit of final drive times gear — and the axis on its
own is chart furniture with no meaning at all.
WHAT THIS RETIRES: every argument in this repo about which axis value is
correct, including this morning's k-agreement argument for 157 and this
afternoon's every-reproducible-tune-says-159 argument. Both were reasoning
about a number that is only half of a measurement.
WHAT REPLACES IT, and it is the only rule the app needs: READ THE AXIS AND
THE FIT ON THE SAME TUNE, IN THE SAME SITTING. Pair them and k comes out
right regardless of what either reads. Mix them and it does not. The July
fixture's 157-or-159 confusion was never an axis problem — it was two
half-measurements filed as if they were one.
theAppsKIsFourPercentLow: AND THIS QUANTIFIES THE SPREAD DEFECT IN THE LIVE WORKFLOW.
Boston reads the fit BEFORE applying the app's tune, so it is read on the
game's gearbox, whose top gear is 0.85. He read about 4.34 — which is why
the app recommended 4.34, since vFrac for road is 1.00 and the
recommendation is the fit itself. The app then built its speed constant
with SPREAD's top ratio instead of the one that was on the car:
what the app computed   159 * 4.34 * 0.82  =  565.9
what it should have     159 * 4.34 * 0.85  =  586.6
what the car actually is, measured on its own gearbox   ~588.3
So the app's k is 3.8% low, and every per-gear speed it printed is 3.8%
low with it. Using the real top ratio of the gearbox the fit was read on
gets within 0.3% of the measured value, which is the whole fix.
CONFIRMATION THAT THE TWO GEARBOXES ARE CONSISTENT, not merely close: the
fit on the game's gearbox was 4.34 and on the app's it is about 4.52, a
ratio of 1.041, against a top-ratio ratio of 0.85/0.82 = 1.037. The fit
moves inversely with the top ratio exactly as k = axis * fit * topRatio
requires. The model is right; only the constant fed into it was wrong.
THE FIX, in order of how well it matches what Boston actually does:
1. Ask for the top ratio of the gearbox the fit was read on, and use it.
One extra number off a screen he is already looking at.
2. Or tell him to re-read the fit after applying the app's ratios, which
is a second trip to the tuning menu for the same information.
Option 1 also stops SPREAD being load-bearing at all, which is worth having
given the table is known wrong for six of its seven rows.
notes: Top speed across the three rows went 140.3, 140.0, 140.4 — non-monotonic again, and 0-100 went 8.983, 8.967, 8.983, which is one frame down and back. Both patterns match the earlier sweep. Given the repeat test showed zero variance within a sitting, these remain real, and nothing in the current model predicts a non-monotonic top speed across 0.01 of final drive. Recorded, unexplained, for the third time.
